## Part 2 · 0:10:52

[0:10:52] To pick just one example, taking quantificational expressions to be ontologically committing is markedly disadvantageous with respect to tensed sentences about no longer existent or not yet existent individuals. Even if some partisans of tensed time deny that future contingent statements are true or false, nevertheless very few have the temerity to deny that past-tensed statements about individuals who do not presently exist are true. For example, it seems indisputably true that there have been 44 US presidents.

[0:11:38] The nonexistence of most of them is no impediment to our quantifying over past US presidents. To infer from the truth of such a statement that time is in fact tenseless and that past and future individuals are on an ontological par with present individuals would be to draw a breathtaking metaphysical inference on the basis of the slim read of the Neo-Quinean criterion of ontological commitment.

[0:12:22] It is noteworthy that in debates over presentism tenseless time theorists tend simply to presuppose without argument that quantification is ontologically committing and so our ability to quantify over past or future individuals in true sentences is taken to commit us to their existence. Thus Theodore Sider muses and I quote "Since ordinary talk and thought are full of quantification over non-present objects presentists are in a familiar predicament.

[0:12:53] In their unreflective moments they apparently commit themselves to far more than their ontological scruples allow." In fact it is only the person rather the only person in a predicament here is the presentist who also accepts that quantification is ontologically committing. It never seems to occur to tenseless time theorists that our ability to quantify over purely past or future individuals in true sentences might be a good reason to reject the criterion of ontological commitment which they unquestioningly presuppose.

[0:13:31] Sider notwithstanding we do speak as if presentism is true, but we do not speak as if quantification is a device of ontological commitment. That is why we freely quantify over merely past objects without thinking that such objects therefore exist. Similar disadvantages of taking quantificational expressions to be ontologically committing also arise with regard to intentional statements, modal statements, and mereological statements. These examples are sufficient in my opinion to warrant rejection of the neo-Quinean view of formal and informal quantifiers. But, that conclusion may remain moot.

[0:14:18] What is important for our purposes, rather, is that these considerations, coupled with the want of any arguments for the truth of the neo-Quinean meta-ontological rules, certainly suffice to show that the neo-Quinean criterion of ontological commitment is far from incumbent upon us, and that therefore the theist may plausibly reject it. Alex Orenstein rightly reminds us that there are fashions in philosophical explications, one of which today is taking first-order existential quantifiers to express metaphysically heavy existence assertions.

[0:15:05] It is perfectly reasonable to buck the fashion trend in this regard. Doing so opens the door for affirming truths like there is a prime number between two and four without commitment to the existence of mathematical objects. Although Quine thought that it is only through quantification that we make ontological commitments, neo-Quineans tend to think that singular terms are also devices of ontological commitment. What is at stake here is one's theory of reference. Two questions arise. First, must singular terms refer to something in order for a sentence featuring them to be true?

[0:15:57] And second, does successful reference imply that there is something in the world which is the referent or denotation of the relevant term? Proponents of the indispensability argument answer yes to both these questions. In contrast, free logicians and neutralists challenge the claim that the use of singular terms in sentences we take to be true is ontologically committing.

[0:16:49] Azzouni denies the crucial assumption underlying both neo-Meinongian and neo-Quinean views that statements involving singular terms, and I quote, "are true or false on the basis of the properties had by the objects referred to by the singular terms appearing in those statements." End quote. Azzouni distinguishes between reference superscript R, um or aboutness R, which is a relation between a term and an object, and reference E, or aboutness E, which is is a relation, but a characterization that applies to empty singular terms in a discourse.

[0:17:25] This distinction allows Azouni to maintain that use of singular terms is ontologically neutral. I quote, "The ordinary words about and refer are neutral between uses of them that indicate genuine relations between language and thought and the world and pseudo relations, terms that have the appearance of relations but aren't." End quote. Azouni differentiates his view from those of the neo-Quinean and the neo-Meinongian who are united in construing reference and aboutness as in every case a relation to an object, whether existent or non-existent.

[0:18:11] For Azouni, reference {e} and aboutness {e} are object-directed in the sense of being intentional, but they are not relations to an object of any sort. So, for example, the singular term "two" does not, in Azouni's view, refer {r} to anything, for there is no object to which this term stands in a relation. But, the term "two" is about {e} the number two in that one's thoughts are two-directed. Azouni is even willing to say, using the ontologically neutral quantifier, that there is something to which we refer {e} and about {e} which we speak.

[0:18:58] But, by such an ontologically irrelevant assertion, he means to indicate merely the object-directedness of our thought and discourse. It seems to me that Azouni is on the right track here. It is a datum of ordinary language that we frequently assert true statements which contain singular terms which do not denote existing objects. Consider the following examples. The weather in Atlanta will be hot today. Sherry's disappointment with her husband was deep and unassuageable. The price of the tickets is £10.

[0:19:44] Wednesday falls between Tuesday and Thursday. His sincerity was touching. James couldn't pay his mortgage. The view of the Jezreel Valley from atop Mount Carmel was breathtaking. Your constant complaining is futile. Spassky's forfeiture ended the match. He did it for my sake and the children's. It would be fantastic to think that all of the singular terms featured in these plausibly true sentences have objects in the world corresponding to them.

[0:20:30] Examples like these are legion. In fact, I have come to suspect that singular terms which refer to real-world objects may actually be the exception rather than the rule in ordinary language. Consider the following paragraph quoted by Michael Dummett from a London daily. Margaret Thatcher yesterday gave her starkest warning yet about the dangers of global warming caused by air pollution.

## Part 3 · 0:21:19

[0:21:19] But, she did not announce any new policy to combat climate change and sea level rises apart from a qualified commitment that Britain would stabilize its emissions of carbon dioxide, the most important greenhouse gas altering the climate by the year 2005. Britain would only fulfill that commitment if other unspecified nations promised similar restraint. Nothing unusual about such discourse, but as Dummett observes, save for Margaret Thatcher, air and sea, there is not a noun or noun phrase in this paragraph incontrovertibly standing for or applying to a concrete object.

[0:21:59] A lightweight Platonist, Dummett is unfazed about postulating objects or reference for such terms. But those who have a more robust sense of reality will be very hesitant about augmenting the world's population so profligately. It seems evident then that not all singular terms in true sentences have corresponding objects in the world. How is it that we are thus able to assert truly sentences with empty singular terms? In order to get at this question, we first need to address the question, do vacuous singular terms refer?

[0:22:48] And in order to answer that question, we need to ask what it is to refer or what is the nature of reference. This question is largely neglected by contemporary theorists. Almost all contemporary theories of reference are actually theories about how to fix reference, rather than theories about the nature of reference itself. The unspoken assumption behind most contemporary theories of reference is the presupposition that reference is a word-world relation. So, the terms which refer must have real-world objects as their denotations.

[0:23:37] In a standard philosophical encyclopedia, for example, Timothy Williamson calls reference the central relation between language or thought and the world. Now, Williamson is right about the importance of reference, but the assumption that reference is a relation begs the question against certain theories of reference. In distinguishing reference R, which is indeed a word-world relation, from reference E, which is a non-relational sort of reference, Azouni challenges this widespread assumption.

[0:24:25] It seems to me, however, that Azouni's evolving views on reference have not yet come to the most satisfactory form. For his reference R is simply what most theorists take reference to be, and his reference E remains unexplicated and mysterious. We are left wondering what it is and how it works. It therefore behooves us to look more deeply into the nature of reference. It is an experiential datum that referring is a speech act carried out by an intentional agent. Words in and of themselves engage in no such activity.

[0:25:13] Lifeless and inert, words are just ink marks on paper or sounds heard by a recipient. Absent an agent, shapes or noises do not refer to anything at all. If, for example, an earthquake were to send several pebbles rolling down a hillside which randomly came to rest in the configuration John loves Suzy, the names, if we would even call them names, would not refer to anybody. An interpreting agent uses his words as a means of referring to something. Referring is thus an intentional activity of persons, and words are mere instruments.

[0:25:59] It is the great merit of the Swedish philosopher Arvid Bove's new deflationary theory of reference that he takes truly seriously the fact, given lip service everywhere, that it is persons who refer to things by means of their words, so that words at best refer only in a derivative sense, if at all. Bove's most significant contribution to our understanding reference is that he furnishes a central schema for reference formulated in terms of the referring activity of persons. And here is his schema R. A refers to B if and only if A says something about B, where A always stands for a speaker.

[0:26:52] Though formulated in terms of persons rather than words, this account is truly deflationary because it does not attempt to tell us anything about the nature of reference itself. It leaves it entirely open whether reference is a relation as Frege and Meinong assumed or whether it is an intentional property of a mind as held by Brentano and Husserl. Taking reference to be a relation between a speaker and some object does make R ontologically committing to either existing or non-existing objects which are the reference of which one speaks.

[0:27:38] But no such commitment is involved for someone who stands in the tradition of Brentano and Husserl in thinking of reference as an intentional activity of agents which may or may not be correlated with real-world objects. So, on Bove's account if I assert 1 + 1 = 2, then I have said something about two. It follows from R that I have thus referred to two. But it does not follow that there is some object whether existent or non-existent as the number two.

[0:28:29] One has the option of avoiding the inference to there is something to which I have referred by restricting with the free logicians existential generalization or the option of granting the inference but rendering it harmless by denying with neutralism that the existential quantifier is ontologically committing. Hence Bove recognizes the neutrality of his theory for the debate between realists and anti-realists. Given schema R, we now ask, what does it mean to say that A says something about B as stipulated by R?

[0:29:11] Bouvay proposes to analyze the expression about and then explain refer in terms of it. He offers the following schema as implicitly defining about. And this is his schema A. That ST is about T. Where S blank is a sentence context with a blank slot for singular terms. Again, Bouvay's account of aboutness is extraordinarily deflationary. It does not tell us what aboutness is, but simply provides a schema for determining what a that clause containing a singular term or presumably terms is about.

[0:30:02] So, for example, that Ponce de Leon sought the fountain of youth is about Ponce de Leon and about the fountain of youth because the singular terms Ponce de Leon and the fountain of youth fill the blanks in the sentence context blank sought blank. Now, since schema A is so deflationary, I do not think we should take A as providing an analysis of aboutness or as serving as an explanation of reference as Bouvay claims. Indeed, taking A to explain schema R seems to get things exactly backwards. The reason why that ST is about T is because T is used by some person to refer to T.

[0:30:50] On an account like Bove's, so-called speaker's reference, what the speaker had in mind becomes paramount. For given schema R, the only genuine referring is that done by the speaker. Rather, schema A merely tells us when someone has said something about something so as to meet the condition laid down in schema R. Bove recognizes that schema A is no more ontologically committing to objects than schema R.

## Part 4 · 0:31:42

[0:31:42] He writes, "A itself is neutral on how to conceive of the position following about in the instances of A, so that we could deny the validity of the inference to there is something such that I have a certain belief about it." End quote. So, if I assert Ponce de Leon sought the fountain of youth, I have said something which is both true and about the fountain of youth as well as about Ponce de Leon, but we are not entitled to infer with Meinong that there is a non-existent object called the fountain of youth which this sentence is about.

[0:32:17] I can, therefore, say things about non-existence like Pegasus, the accident that was prevented, holes in the cheese, or numbers without committing myself to there being objects about which I am speaking. This accords with the nature of intentionality, since intentional states of mind are not always about real world objects. By construing reference in terms of the referring activity of persons and understanding aboutness in terms of intentionality, we make an advance over Azouni's views to arrive at a more satisfactory neutralist account.

[0:33:02] This account is consistent with anti-realism because successful singular reference does not require that there be objects in the world which stand in some sort of relation to a speaker's words. Now, of course, sometimes objects answering to the terms we use do exist, but in a surprisingly large number of cases, as our earlier example showed, there are no such objects. That does not stop us from talking about them or referring to them, for these activities are, at least in such cases, purely intentional activities.

[0:33:50] Not only does the use of singular terms in sentences we take to be true seem to be non-committing ontologically, but just as there are disadvantages to taking first-order quantification to be existentially loaded, so there are also disadvantages to taking reference in true sentences to carry existential implications.

[0:34:34] Karel Lambert, one of the pioneers of free logic, complains that although modern logic in the late 19th century shed itself of various existence assumptions implicit in Aristotelian logic with respect to the use of general terms, modern logic remains infected with existence assumptions with respect to the use of singular terms, assumptions that should not characterize a purely formal discipline. These existence assumptions regarding singular terms surface dramatically in the way in which standard modern logic handles identity statements.

[0:35:01] For such statements cannot be true according to standard logic unless the reference of the singular terms employed in such statements exist. In other words, identity statements are ontologically committing for anyone who asserts them. But it seems bizarre to think that from a seemingly trivial truth of the form T is identical to T, where T is some singular term, it follows that the thing denoted by T actually exists. Nevertheless, this is what standard logic requires.

[0:35:49] For it follows from the identity statement A is identical to A that there is some X such that X is identical to A, or in other words, that something is identical with A. For neo-Quineans with their existentially loaded quantifiers, there is some X such that X is identical to A just is the symbolization of X exists. Lambert takes this ontological implication of mere identity statements to be absurd. For it would follow from the fact that Vulcan is identical to Vulcan that there is some object identical with Vulcan. That is to say that Vulcan exists.

[0:36:29] Standard logic avoids this untoward result by treating all identity statements with vacuous sing- singular terms as false. So, standard logic must regard a statement like Vulcan is identical to Vulcan as false, even though it appears to be a tautology, which is necessarily true. Standard logic cannot therefore distinguish the truth value of identity statements like Zeus is identical to Zeus and Zeus is identical to Allah. Yet, the first seems to be necessarily true, and the second obviously false.

[0:37:14] Nor can standard logic affirm the truth of Aristotle is identical to Aristotle, or Churchill is identical to Churchill, since Aristotle and Churchill no longer exist, and so there are no things with which they can be identical. As I said before, it would be the height of ontological presumption to claim that the truth of such seemingly trivial statements implies a tenseless theory of time, according to which all persons throughout time are equally existent.

[0:37:51] Such an inference would only underscore the free logician's claim that modern logic is still infected with inappropriate existence assumptions. As a result of its existence assumptions with respect to singular terms, standard logic becomes limited in its application to certain inferences and does not permit us to discriminate between uh inferences where the referentiality of the terms is crucial and those where it is not. For example, we are prohibited from inferring Abraham Lincoln was the great emancipator. Abraham Lincoln brooded, therefore the great emancipator brooded.

[0:38:32] An inference whose obvious validity should not be dependent on Lincoln's existing. Moreover, one would think that the methods of logic should apply to reasoning involving singular terms, which for all we know may or may not refer to existing objects. For example, astronomers used the term Vulcan for the suspected planet between Mercury and the Sun before knowing whether such a planet existed or not. Free logician John Nolt observes that the obligation to establish the existence of things before naming them is so irksome that, and I quote, "Even mathematicians routinely flout it.

[0:39:21] They get away with this usually only by being discreetly inexplicit about the underlying logic, which is in consequence not rigorously classical." End quote. Advocates of positive free logic maintain that certain sentences can be truly asserted even though they contain vacuous singular terms. This feature of positive free logic strikes me as well motivated and eminently plausible. The truth of identity statements involving vacuous singular terms is of a piece with the evident truth of many sentences which feature vacuous singular terms.

[0:40:07] Free logic's denial that the use of singular terms in sentences we take to be true is ontologically committing for their user is, I think a step in the right direction. But because free logic takes the existential quantifier of first-order logic to carry existence commitments it cannot avoid the platonistic commitments of much abstract object talk such as there are prime numbers greater than 100. Better to adopt a consistent neutralism. According to which first-order quantifiers as well as singular terms are not ontologically committing.

[0:40:52] Such a neutral logic will not technically be speaking be a free logic. But as Alex Orenstein asks isn't a logic which dissociates the quantifiers from existence a paradigm of a logic that is free of existence assumptions? In my opinion the criterion of ontological commitment that comes to expression in premise one of the indispensability argument is not only false but I should say obviously false and utterly implausible. It is a metaontological thesis for which there is no good argument and the linguistic evidence is overwhelmingly against it. Its assumption hinders logical reasoning.
